lessons.title: Overview of Pork Primal Cuts
lessons.body: Pork primal cuts are the large sections a butcher creates when breaking down a whole pig. In Africa, common primals include the shoulder (often called Boston butt or picnic), loin, belly, leg (ham), and sometimes the head and jowl. Each primal yields specific retail cuts. The shoulder is tough but flavorful, ideal for slow cooking or sausage. The loin runs along the back and gives chops, roasts, and tenderloin. The belly is fatty and used for bacon. The leg is lean and used for fresh hams or cured ham. Understanding these primals helps you plan how to cut a carcass efficiently. A typical market-weight pig in Africa weighs 60â90 kg dressed. From that, expect about 20% shoulder, 20% loin, 15% belly, 25% leg, and the rest in offal, fat, and bone. Tools needed: a sharp breaking knife (8â10 inch), a bone saw, a meat hook, and a clean cutting table. Always work in a cool room (below 10Â°C) if possible. Start by splitting the carcass down the spine. Then remove the head, feet, and internal fat. Next, separate the shoulder from the loin by cutting between the 4th and 5th ribs. Remove the loin from the leg by cutting at the hip joint. Finally, remove the belly from the loin by cutting along the rib ends. Label and store each primal properly. This overview sets the foundation for the next lessons.

lessons.title: Breaking Down a Whole Pork Carcass
lessons.body: Breaking down a whole pork carcass is heavy work but follows a logical sequence. You need a sturdy rail or table, a meat saw, a breaking knife, a boning knife, a sharpening steel, and a clean apron. Start with a carcass that has been chilled for 24 hours at 0â4Â°C. First, place the carcass on its back. Remove the head by cutting through the atlas joint (between skull and first neck vertebra). Save the head for head cheese or stock. Remove the feet at the hock joint using a saw. Next, split the carcass lengthwise down the spine using a saw or cleaver. You now have two sides. For each side, remove the leaf fat (kidney fat) and set aside for lard. Remove the kidneys and liver if still present. Now separate the shoulder: cut between the 4th and 5th ribs, then through the shoulder joint. The shoulder includes the picnic and Boston butt. Next, remove the loin by cutting along the rib ends from the shoulder to the hip. The loin runs from the last rib to the hip bone. Then remove the belly by cutting just below the ribs, leaving the loin intact. Finally, separate the leg (ham) from the loin by cutting through the hip joint. You now have primal cuts: shoulder, loin, belly, leg, and miscellaneous parts like ribs, jowl, and hocks. Weigh each primal to track yield. A 80 kg carcass should yield about 16 kg shoulder, 16 kg loin, 12 kg belly, 20 kg leg, and 16 kg of bones, fat, and offal. Clean your tools and table with hot soapy water after. This breakdown is the core skill of pork fabrication.

lessons.title: Cutting Pork Chops and Roasts
lessons.body: Pork chops come from the loin. After removing the loin primal, you have a long muscle with a bone (the rib or spine) on one side. Decide whether to keep it bone-in or boneless. Bone-in chops are more flavorful and common in African markets. To cut chops, first trim the loin of excess fat, leaving about 1 cm of fat cap. Remove the tenderloin if still attached (it sits on the inner side). For bone-in chops, use a meat saw to cut perpendicular to the spine, about 2.5â3 cm thick. For boneless chops, run your knife along the bones to remove the entire rack, then cut the eye of meat into 2.5 cm slices. A standard chop weighs 150â200 g. For roasts, cut larger sections: a bone-in loin roast is 4â6 ribs long (about 1.5â2 kg). A boneless loin roast is the eye of meat tied with butcher twine at 2 cm intervals. Season or marinate as desired. In Africa, popular dry rubs include paprika, garlic, and chili. For a simple roast, rub with salt, pepper, and crushed garlic, then roast at 180Â°C for 25 minutes per 500 g until internal temperature reaches 63Â°C. Let rest 10 minutes before slicing. Chops can be grilled, pan-fried, or braised. For tough chops, brine in salt water (50 g salt per liter) for 2 hours before cooking. Always cut against the grain for tenderness. Store chops and roasts wrapped in butcher paper or vacuum-sealed at 0â4Â°C for up to 5 days, or freeze for 3 months.

lessons.title: Producing Bacon and Ham from the Belly and Leg
lessons.body: Bacon comes from the pork belly. Start with a fresh belly, skin on or off. For dry-cured bacon, mix 25 g curing salt (containing 6.25% sodium nitrite) with 250 g sea salt, 100 g sugar, and 10 g black pepper for a 5 kg belly. Rub the mixture all over the belly. Place in a food-grade plastic bag or non-reactive container. Refrigerate at 2â4Â°C for 7 days, flipping daily. The belly will release liquid; that's normal. After curing, rinse well and pat dry. For smoked bacon, cold smoke at 20â25Â°C for 6â8 hours using wood chips (hickory or apple). If you don't have a smoker, you can oven-bake at 90Â°C for 2 hours to set the cure, then slice. Slice bacon 2â3 mm thick. For ham, use the leg primal. You can make fresh ham (roast) or cured ham. For a wet-cured ham, prepare a brine: 1.5 kg salt, 500 g sugar, 50 g curing salt, and 10 liters water for a 5 kg leg. Inject brine into the leg along the bone and around joints. Submerge the leg in brine and keep at 2â4Â°C for 5 days per kg (so a 5 kg leg cures for 25 days). Then rinse and smoke at 75â85Â°C until internal temperature reaches 68Â°C. In Africa, many artisans use local spices like cloves, bay leaves, and chili in the brine. Always use food-grade curing salts; never use industrial nitrites. After curing, ham can be sliced or left whole. Store bacon and ham in the fridge for 2 weeks or freeze for 6 months.

lessons.title: Preparing Ribs and Tenderloin
lessons.body: Pork ribs come from the belly side of the loin. There are two main types: baby back ribs (from the loin) and spare ribs (from the belly). After removing the loin, you'll find the rib rack attached to the belly. To prepare spare ribs, trim the belly to leave a rectangular rack of ribs with about 2 cm of meat on top. Remove the membrane on the bone side by slipping a knife under it and pulling it off. This makes the ribs more tender. Cut the rack into individual portions or leave whole. For baby back ribs, they are the curved ribs attached to the loin. Remove the loin meat first, then separate the ribs. A typical rack has 10â13 ribs. Season with a dry rub (paprika, brown sugar, salt, pepper, garlic powder) and let sit for 30 minutes. Cook low and slow: smoke at 110Â°C for 4â5 hours, or bake at 150Â°C for 2.5 hours, until meat pulls back from the bone. For tenderloin, it's the long, lean muscle on the inside of the loin. Remove it by pulling it away from the loin with your fingers, then trim off silver skin. A whole tenderloin weighs 300â500 g. Cut into medallions 2 cm thick, or leave whole for roasting. Marinate in soy sauce, garlic, and ginger for 2 hours, then grill or pan-sear for 3â4 minutes per side. Tenderloin is very lean, so don't overcook. In Africa, serve with rice, plantains, or chapati. Store ribs and tenderloin at 0â4Â°C for up to 3 days.

lessons.title: Utilizing Pork Offal and By-Products
lessons.body: Pork offal includes liver, heart, kidneys, tongue, head, feet, intestines, and blood. These are nutritious and can be profitable. Start with the liver: soak in milk or salt water for 1 hour to remove bitterness. Slice 1 cm thick, dredge in flour, and pan-fry with onions and chili. Heart and tongue: simmer in salted water for 2 hours until tender, then slice for sandwiches or stews. Kidneys: remove the white core, slice, and soak in vinegar water for 30 minutes, then fry with garlic. Feet and hocks: rich in collagen, perfect for slow-cooked soups or pickled feet. Clean thoroughly by scrubbing with salt and vinegar, then boil for 3 hours. Head: make head cheese by boiling the head with spices, picking the meat, and setting in gelatinous broth. Intestines: clean by turning inside out, scraping, and soaking in salt water; use as sausage casings. Blood: collect fresh, stir to prevent clotting, and make blood sausage (black pudding) with onions, fat, and spices. Fat: render leaf fat and back fat into lard by slowly heating at 100Â°C for 2 hours; strain and store. Lard is used for cooking or soap making. Bones: simmer for 6â12 hours to make pork stock. In Africa, offal is often sold at lower prices but can be value-added into ready-to-eat products. Always handle offal with strict hygiene: keep at 0â4Â°C, cook thoroughly to 71Â°C, and never mix with cooked meat. Properly used, offal can increase your carcass profit by 15â20%.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pork Fabrication for African Butcheries

Pork fabrication is the process of breaking a whole pig carcass into primal cuts, sub-primals, retail cuts, and value-added products. In an African butchery context, mastery of pork fabrication directly affects your margins: a skilled butcher can extract 8â15% more saleable yield from the same carcass compared to an untrained operator. This practical reference consolidates the core knowledge from the six lessons in this module into a single working document for butchers, shop owners, and meat processors operating in African markets.

Whether you are supplying wet markets in Nairobi, hotels in Lagos, or retail packs in Lusaka, the principles remain constant: understand the anatomy, control the temperature, minimise waste, and convert every part of the carcass into revenue. Pork is one of the fastest-growing meat categories in sub-Saharan Africa, driven by urbanisation, rising incomes, and the expansion of commercial pig production in countries such as Uganda, Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa. This reference is designed to help you capture that demand profitably.

Understanding Yield and Carcass Value

The commercial reality of pork fabrication is that your profit is determined before the first cut is made. A whole pork carcass typically yields 65â75% saleable meat after slaughter and chilling, depending on fat cover, breed, and butchering skill. In African markets where feed costs are high and consumer purchasing power varies, maximising yield from every carcass is essential.

Table 1 below provides a practical yield reference for a typical 90 kg live-weight pig, which produces a carcass of approximately 65â70 kg. Use these figures to price your cuts and to negotiate with suppliers.

Table 1: Indicative primal cut yields from a 90 kg live-weight pig (carcass ~68 kg)
Primal Cut Approx. Weight (kg) % of Carcass Primary Retail Products Typical African Market Use
Shoulder (Boston Butt / Picnic) 14â17 20â25% Roasts, steaks, mince, sausage Nyama choma, stewing, sausages
Loin (Loin, Tenderloin, Ribs) 14â17 20â25% Chops, roasts, ribs, tenderloin Hotel & restaurant cuts, braai
Belly (Side) 10â14 15â20% Bacon, ribs, roasting pieces Bacon, value-added processing
Leg (Fresh Ham) 15â18 22â27% Ham, roasts, schnitzel, mince Ham, deli meats, festive roasts
Offal & By-Products 5â8 8â12% Liver, heart, kidney, trotters, head Local delicacies, pet food, stock
Total Saleable 58â74 85â95% â â

Sources: FAO Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (1994); USDA IMPS Series 400; MLA Pork Carcass Specifications. Figures are indicative and will vary with breed, age, and fat cover.

Cutting Pork Chops and Roasts

The loin is the highest-value primal in most African butcheries. To cut consistent chops, first remove the loin from the carcass, trim the fat cover to 5â8 mm, and square the ends. Chops should be cut 2â3 cm thick for retail and 3â4 cm for restaurant supply. For roasts, cut 8â12 cm sections from the rib end (rib roast) or the sirloin end (loin roast).

Bone-in chops command a premium in most markets because customers associate them with flavour and value. However, boneless loin cuts are preferred by hotels and catering operations. Decide your cut profile based on your customer base, not on habit.

Producing Bacon and Ham

Bacon is produced from the belly through curing (wet or dry), optional smoking, and slicing. Ham is produced from the leg through curing, smoking, or cooking. Both are high-margin products that extend shelf life and reduce waste. In African markets, bacon and ham are increasingly demanded by urban supermarkets, hotels, and fast-food outlets.

Table 2 below summarises the curing and processing parameters for bacon and ham production at small-to-medium scale.

Table 2: Curing and processing parameters for bacon and ham
Parameter Bacon (Belly) Ham (Leg)
Cure type Wet brine or dry rub Wet brine or dry rub
Salt concentration 2.5â3.5% of meat weight 3.0â4.0% of meat weight
Cure time (chilled, 2â4Â°C) 3â7 days 7â14 days (or 24â48 hrs if injected)
Nitrite (as NaNOâ) 100â150 ppm 100â150 ppm
Smoking temperature 50â60Â°C (hot smoke) 60â75Â°C (hot smoke) or cold smoke 20â25Â°C
Internal cook temperature Not required (sliced raw) 68â72Â°C for cooked ham
Storage (vacuum-packed) 0â4Â°C, 4â6 weeks 0â4Â°C, 6â8 weeks

Sources: FAO Guidelines for Meat Processing; USDA FSIS Processing Inspectors' Calculations Handbook; Codex Alimentarius CAC/RCP 13-1976 (revised) Code of Hygienic Practice for Meat.

Preparing Ribs and Tenderloin

Ribs are cut from the belly side of the loin (spare ribs) or from the loin itself (baby back ribs). Remove the membrane from the bone side, trim excess fat, and cut into uniform racks. Tenderloin is removed from the loin and trimmed of silver skin. It is the most tender cut on the pig and should be sold whole or as medallions to premium customers.

In African markets, ribs are increasingly popular for grilling and braai. Tenderloin is a hotel and restaurant cut. Price both according to their premium positioning, not as generic pork.

Utilising Offal and By-Products

Offal â liver, heart, kidney, tongue, trotters, head, and blood â is a significant revenue stream in most African butcheries. In many communities, these products are culturally valued and command good prices. Do not treat them as waste. Clean, chill, and display them properly. Trotters and head can be sold for soups and stews; liver and kidney for grills and stews; blood for traditional dishes.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Cold Chain and Hygiene

Pork must be kept at or below 4Â°C from slaughter to sale. Above 4Â°C, Salmonella, Listeria, and Yersinia multiply rapidly. Never leave carcasses or cuts at ambient temperature for more than 2 hours. In hot African climates, this window is shorter â use insulated boxes, ice, or refrigerated transport at all times. Cook pork to a minimum internal temperature of 63Â°C (medium) or 71Â°C (well done) to eliminate parasites such as Taenia solium and Trichinella. Wash hands, knives, and surfaces between handling raw and cooked product. Failure to maintain the cold chain is the single largest cause of meat spoilage and foodborne illness in small butcheries.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Verify cold chain: Carcass temperature must be â¤4Â°C before fabrication begins. Check with a calibrated probe thermometer.
  • Sanitise tools: Knives, saws, chopping blocks, and hands must be cleaned and sanitised before and between cuts.
  • Follow the primal sequence: Shoulder â Loin â Belly â Leg â Offal. This reduces cross-contamination and improves yield.
  • Trim fat to spec: 5â8 mm on loin, 8â10 mm on shoulder, 10â15 mm on belly for bacon. Consistent trim builds customer trust.
  • Weigh and record: Record the weight of each primal and retail cut. Track yield against Table 1 to identify losses.
  • Label and date: Every pack must carry product name, weight, date, and storage temperature. This is a legal requirement in most African markets and a marketing advantage.
  • Separate offal immediately: Chill offal within 30 minutes of removal. Do not leave it on the cutting table.
  • Clean down: At the end of fabrication, wash floors, walls, tables, and equipment. Document the cleaning in your hygiene log.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (free, official)
  • FAO â Guidelines for Meat Processing (free, official)
  • USDA FSIS â Processing Inspectors' Calculations Handbook (free, official)
  • Codex Alimentarius â Codes of Practice for Meat (free, official)
  • WOAH â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (meat hygiene chapter) (free, official)

Business takeaway: Pork fabrication is not just a butchery skill â it is a profit discipline. Every gram of trim, every offal item, and every degree of temperature control has a direct effect on your bottom line. Train your staff, document your yields, and treat the cold chain as sacred. In the growing African pork market, the butcher who fabricates with precision and sells with consistency will outperform the competition every time.

quiz.q: Which primal cut is used to make bacon?
quiz.explanation: Bacon is made from the pork belly, which is the fatty cut from the underside of the pig.

quiz.q: What is the typical dressed weight of a market-weight pig in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A typical market-weight pig in Africa weighs 60â90 kg after dressing.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for splitting a pork carcass down the spine?
quiz.explanation: A meat saw is used to cut through bone when splitting the carcass.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you chill a pork carcass before breaking it down?
quiz.explanation: Chilling at 0â4Â°C firms the meat and reduces bacterial growth.

quiz.q: Where do you cut to separate the shoulder from the loin?
quiz.explanation: The shoulder is separated from the loin by cutting between the 4th and 5th ribs.

quiz.q: What is the leaf fat used for?
quiz.explanation: Leaf fat is the kidney fat and is rendered into high-quality lard.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of a pork chop?
quiz.explanation: Pork chops are typically cut 2.5â3 cm thick for even cooking.

quiz.q: How long should you brine pork chops to improve tenderness?
quiz.explanation: A 2-hour brine in salt water helps tenderize and season the chops.

quiz.q: What internal temperature should a pork roast reach?
quiz.explanation: Pork should be cooked to a safe internal temperature of 63Â°C.

quiz.q: Which curing salt is used for making bacon?
options: B) Curing salt with 6.25% sodium nitrite
quiz.explanation: Curing salt containing sodium nitrite prevents botulism and gives bacon its color.

quiz.q: How long should a 5 kg pork belly cure for bacon?
quiz.explanation: A 5 kg belly typically cures for 7 days in the refrigerator, flipping daily.

quiz.q: What is the typical smoking temperature for cold-smoked bacon?
quiz.explanation: Cold smoking at 20â25Â°C flavors the bacon without cooking it.

quiz.q: How long should a 5 kg leg cure in brine for ham?
quiz.explanation: A 5 kg leg cures for 5 days per kg, so 25 days total.

quiz.q: What is the internal temperature for cooked ham?
quiz.explanation: Ham is cooked until it reaches an internal temperature of 68Â°C.

quiz.q: Which type of ribs are called baby back ribs?
quiz.explanation: Baby back ribs are the curved ribs attached to the loin.

quiz.q: Why should you remove the membrane from the bone side of ribs?
options: B) It makes the ribs more tender
quiz.explanation: Removing the membrane allows seasonings to penetrate and makes the ribs more tender.

quiz.q: What is the typical weight of a whole pork tenderloin?
quiz.explanation: A whole pork tenderloin typically weighs 300â500 g.

quiz.q: How long should you marinate pork tenderloin before grilling?
quiz.explanation: A 2-hour marinade is sufficient to flavor the lean tenderloin.

quiz.q: Which offal item is often used as sausage casings?
quiz.explanation: Cleaned pig intestines are used as natural sausage casings.

quiz.q: How do you remove bitterness from pork liver?
options: B) Soak in milk or salt water
quiz.explanation: Soaking liver in milk or salt water helps draw out bitterness.

quiz.q: What is head cheese made from?
quiz.explanation: Head cheese is a meat jelly made from the meat of a pig's head.

quiz.q: What temperature should you render lard at?
quiz.explanation: Lard is rendered slowly at around 100Â°C to avoid burning.

quiz.q: How long should you simmer bones to make pork stock?
quiz.explanation: Simmering bones for 6â12 hours extracts maximum flavor and gelatin.

quiz.q: What is the safe internal temperature for cooked pork offal?
quiz.explanation: Offal should be cooked to at least 71Â°C to ensure safety.

quiz.q: How much can proper offal utilization increase carcass profit?
quiz.explanation: Value-added offal products can increase profit by 15â20%.

quiz.q: Which spice is commonly used in African dry rubs for pork?
quiz.explanation: Paprika is a common ingredient in African dry rubs for pork.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store pork chops in the refrigerator?
options: A) In a bowl of water
D) In a plastic bag with air
quiz.explanation: Wrapping in butcher paper prevents moisture loss and contamination.

quiz.q: How long can you freeze pork roasts?
quiz.explanation: Pork roasts can be frozen for up to 3 months for best quality.

quiz.q: What is the first step in breaking down a whole pork carcass?
quiz.explanation: The head is removed first by cutting through the atlas joint.

quiz.q: Which primal cut is the leanest?
quiz.explanation: The loin is the leanest primal cut, especially the tenderloin.
